title: Prefill microkernel: speculative inline normalization + delta-encoded session prefix store
creator: Anika Bose
description: Goal: Reduce CPU and end-to-end prefill latency by introducing a lightweight prefill microkernel that speculatively applies inline ASCII/normalize fast-paths and materializes a compact delta-encoded per-session prefix store to avoid repeated full tokenization for common prompt suffixes. This ticket covers design, implementation, benchmarking, and rollout plan for the microkernel shim that routes requests to either the speculatively-optimized path or the full tokenizer.
tasks: Design spec and API for microkernel shim that sits before tokenizer stage
Implement ASCII-dominant inline normalization + fallback to full unicode normalizer
Add delta-encoded per-session prefix store with LRU eviction and compact serialization
Integrate microkernel with prefill scheduler to surface fast-path eligibility and hinting
Add unit and fuzz tests to cover normalization edge-cases and fallback correctness
Benchmark end-to-end on small/medium/large contexts and collect cost/latency metrics
Prepare canary rollout plan and console observability (fast-path hit rate, errors, CPU savings)
acceptance_criteria: 1) Microkernel reduces avg prefill CPU per request by >=20% on ASCII-heavy workloads without regressions on UTF-8 inputs. 2) Fast-path correctness verified across multilingual unit tests and fuzz runs. 3) Observability surfaces fast-path hit rate, fallback reasons, and delta-store evictions. 4) Canary rollout on 5% traffic with automated rollback on quality or latency regressions.
notes: Design trade-offs: compact delta store reduces memory but requires extra small CPU for decoding; prefer CPU if we save >15% end-to-end.
Speculative normalization: optimistic ASCII-path assumes no combining chars; must record a validation checksum to detect mis-normalized inputs and trigger safe fallback.
Eviction policy: session-scoped LRU with token-count budget; keep per-session state under 2KB by default to avoid NUMA thrashing.
Rollout guardrails: tie canary to quality metrics computed by real-eval sets and prompt-level acceptance thresholds in console.
benchmarks: Local bench on p4d.24xlarge: ASCII-heavy synthetic prompts (avg len 320 bytes) => CPU prefill cycles down 28%, median prefill latency down 18ms
Mixed-language bench: no statistical regression on correctness; fast-path hit-rate ~62% for our default english-heavy traffic sample
End-to-end cost simulation: projected 12% token-serving cost savings at 50% fast-path adoption due to reduced prefill CPU billing and lower contention on batch workers
